chapters.category: Ethiopic textual tradition • Modern English research translation
chapters.title: Chapter 87 — The Earth Cries Out and Heavenly Messengers Come
chapters.sourceNote: Translated afresh into clear modern English from the early Greek witness P.Oxy. XVII 2069, fragments 1v–2v, for its surviving portions of 1 Enoch 87:1–3, and from the complete Ethiopic (Geʽez) text in August Dillmann’s 1851 critical edition, Liber Henoch Aethiopice, printed pages 62–63, for the full four-verse chapter and all wording absent from the Greek fragments. The Geʽez text on page 63 reads that one white figure came forth and three came with him; that attested wording is retained here without importing a different numerical reading. No modern English translation was used as the translation base, no commentary was used as Scripture, and no text absent from the primary witnesses was supplied.

verses.text: Again I saw them, and they began to gore one another and devour one another. Then the earth began to cry out.
verses.study: The violence has become mutual and unrestrained: the creatures turn on one another while the earth itself gives voice to the wrong. The cry marks a transition from suffering below to an answer arriving from heaven.
crossReferences: Genesis 4:10 — shed blood cries out from the ground
Genesis 6:11–13 — violence fills the earth and comes before God

verses.text: I raised my eyes again toward heaven and saw in the vision. Look, figures like white men came out from heaven: one came forth from that place, and three came with him.
verses.study: Enoch’s gaze turns upward as heavenly agents enter the vision in humanlike, white appearance. The movement answers the earth’s cry and signals that the violence below has not escaped heaven’s notice.
crossReferences: Genesis 18:1–2 — heavenly visitors appear in the form of men
Daniel 7:9–10 — heavenly attendants stand before the divine court

verses.text: The three who came afterward took hold of my hand. They lifted me away from the generations of the earth and raised me onto a high place. They showed me a tower high above the earth, and all the hills were lower than it.
verses.study: The three heavenly figures remove Enoch from the threatened generations and give him a vantage point above the earth. The lofty tower becomes a protected place of witness from which coming judgment can be seen in its proper scale.
crossReferences: Ezekiel 40:1–2 — the prophet is set on a very high mountain and shown a structure
Revelation 21:10 — the seer is carried to a high mountain to behold God’s work

verses.text: They said to me, ‘Remain here until you see everything that will come upon these elephants, camels, and donkeys, and upon the stars and all the cattle.’
verses.study: Enoch is commanded to stay and observe the full outcome for every group in the vision. The instruction makes him a patient witness: neither the violent offspring, the rebellious stars, nor the cattle will stand outside the judgment about to unfold.
crossReferences: Habakkuk 2:1–3 — the prophet takes his stand to watch and await the appointed vision
Daniel 12:5–6 — the seer remains beside heavenly figures and hears what will follow

explanation.heading: Chapter teaching and context
paragraphs: Chapter 87 brings the violence of Chapter 86 to its crisis. The hybrid creatures gore and consume one another, while the earth’s cry presents creation not as a silent setting but as a witness against bloodshed.

Heaven responds by sending white, humanlike figures. Their arrival shows that divine justice is not indifferent or remote. The text does not yet narrate the sentence; it first establishes that the suffering has been heard and that appointed agents have come.

Three of the figures lift Enoch to a high tower. Separation from the earthly generations protects him and equips him to see what is coming. Revelation here is a responsibility to remain, watch and preserve truthful testimony through the judgment.

The final command includes every class of figure introduced in the vision: the violent offspring, the fallen stars and the cattle. The chapter therefore holds rebellion, its destructive fruit and the suffering world together under one coming divine reckoning.

crossReferences: Genesis 4:10 — the earth bears witness to shed blood
Genesis 6:11–13 — violence throughout the earth brings judgment
Genesis 18:1–2 — heavenly messengers appear as men
Ezekiel 40:1–2 — a prophet is lifted to a high place and shown a structure
Habakkuk 2:1–3 — the prophet stands watch for the appointed vision
Revelation 21:10 — a seer is carried to a high mountain to behold
